summary:
Muğla, the province containing Bodrum, Marmaris and Fethiye, stands under the national framework of Turkey. Turkey has permitted transgender people to change their legal gender since 1988, but only on condition of sex-reassignment surgery, a medical examination and court permission. Turkish marriage law determines eligibility by the gender recorded in a person's civil registry rather than by trans status, so a visitor who has legally changed registered gender may marry a partner of the opposite registered gender. Same-sex marriage, civil unions and adoption are not available in Turkey, and there is no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity.

When the 12th judicial reform package passed in 2026, provisions discriminating against LGBTQ people were removed from the bill, though it made symbolic same-sex weddings possible that carry no legal marital status. Whether the package has since been amended or supplemented is unresolved in the sources.

HRW (World Report 2024, covering 2023) records that the Erdoğan government made anti-LGBT hate speech a core part of its election campaign, and that the ninth successive ban on Istanbul Pride week events in June was accompanied by police arrests of those who attempted to assemble. Authorities regularly and arbitrarily ban other events by LGBT groups, and local authorities around the country have increasingly cancelled concerts by artists openly supportive of LGBT rights; TV regulator RTÜK has justified fines on digital platforms for LGBT-related content as violating 'societal and cultural values.' These nationwide enforcement patterns reach resort-province institutions like Muğla's, coloring what any visible LGBT assembly there can expect.
tangentialFactors:
The 2026 judicial reform package's removal of explicitly discriminatory provisions from the bill, alongside its creation of symbolic same-sex weddings without legal marital status, marks a shift in how the state frames LGBTQ rights even as substantive protections remain absent.

Nationwide patterns of event bans and RTÜK content fines indicate that cultural and public-assembly exposure is driven by central government messaging rather than by any single province's local policy, so Muğla's institutions are unlikely to diverge from the national posture.
localsOnly:
Trans residents of Muğla may change their legal gender under the conditions in force since 1988: sex-reassignment surgery, a medical examination and court permission. Once registered gender is changed, marriage eligibility follows the civil registry entry, permitting marriage to a partner of the opposite registered gender.

Residents have no statutory discrimination protection on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and same-sex marriage, civil unions and adoption remain unavailable. The 2026 judicial reform package removed provisions that had discriminated against LGBTQ people from the bill, but did not establish affirmative protections.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the 12th judicial reform package has been amended, challenged or supplemented since passage in 2026 is unresolved in the sources.

The sources do not document Muğla-specific enforcement incidents, local police practice, or province-level administrative decisions on LGBT events; the enforcement picture is drawn from nationwide patterns reported by HRW.
